title: Single-cell Sequencing Reveals Multi-omics Dynamics During Lymph Node Metastasis in Breast Cancer
authors: Gao Y, Tang C, Guo X, et al.
abstract: Single-cell sequencing and analysis have advanced our understanding of intra-tumoral heterogeneity for breast cancer lymph node metastasis. However, how alterations at multi-omics levels coordinate together in a single tumor cell to drive metastasis remains unclear. Here we performed single-cell multi-omics sequencing of paired primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes from breast cancer patients. This enabled a comprehensive reconstruction of dynamic molecular landscapes by simultaneously profiling genome, epigenome and transcriptome in the same single tumor cell. During metastasis of patients with higher heterogeneity, clonal evolution analysis based on copy number variations at single-cell resolution showed a specific clone possessing metastatic advantages. Meanwhile, the genome-wide DNA methylation underwent stageable changes. In contrast, gene expression was specifically reprogrammed concentrated at tumor cell transition, suggesting a remodelling by organ microenvironment. By integrative multi-omics analysis, we identified genes that were dysregulated at more than one omics, and showed the importance of SLC39A6, ELP2 and RPL13 genes in breast cancer metastasis or prognosis. Our study traces the genomic, epigenomic and transcriptomic dynamics simultaneously from primary tumors to metastatic lymph nodes in the same single cell, providing new insights into breast cancer metastasis.

title: In vitro phenotyping and genomics: a conceptual framework linking plant tissue culture with GWAS, QTL mapping, and multi-omics
authors: Isak MA, Fatima S, Haider I, et al.
abstract: Main conclusion Standardized in vitro phenotypes provide genetically tractable traits that integrate GWAS, QTL mapping, and multi-omics, enabling mechanistic insight and genetics-informed improvement of plant regeneration. Plant tissue culture (PTC) has traditionally been employed as a technical tool for propagation, transformation, and germplasm conservation. This review reframes in vitro culture systems as quantitative phenotyping platforms that enable rigorous genetic dissection of complex traits, such as regeneration competence, stress tolerance, and developmental plasticity. By operating under highly standardized and reproducible conditions, in vitro systems reduce environmental noise and expose genotype-dependent variation that is often obscured in field or greenhouse experiments. When formalized as quantitative traits, culture responses, including callus induction, organogenesis, somatic embryogenesis, and stress survival, become amenable to genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping. Synthesizing evidence across diverse plant species, this review demonstrates that in vitro traits are genetically structured, polygenic, and biologically meaningful, reflecting coordinated regulation of hormonal signaling, chromatin accessibility, stress response pathways, and developmental gene networks. Numerous GWAS and QTL studies have identified loci and candidate genes underlying regeneration efficiency, embryogenic competence, and stress-responsive culture performance, confirming that tissue culture responsiveness is rooted in genomic architecture rather than protocol effects alone. The interpretive power of genetic mapping is substantially enhanced through integration with bioinformatic and multi-omics layers, including transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and network-based analyses, thereby refining candidate prioritization and facilitating mechanistic inference. This review further examines the dual role of somaclonal variation as both a constraint on clonal fidelity and a source of genetic and epigenetic diversity that can reveal cryptic genotype-phenotype relationships. Emphasis is placed on study design principles, phenotyping challenges, statistical modeling strategies, and integrative pipelines that connect genotype to in vitro phenotype and ultimately to breeding and biotechnology applications. This synthesis highlights in vitro culture systems as powerful, genetics-informed platforms for precision breeding, gene validation, and supporting efforts to more predictably and rationally manipulate complex traits, particularly in horticultural and clonally propagated crops.

title: High-efficiency antimony biomineralization by Serratia nematodiphila: process optimization and integrated genomic-transcriptomic-proteomic analysis
authors: Zhou Z, Zhang P, Li Q, et al.
abstract: This study aims to elucidate the transcriptional, protein expression and mineral crystallization response mechanisms of the Serratia nematodiphila strain during the process of converting Sb 3+ into Sb 2 O 3 through integrating multi-omics methods and various mineral analysis techniques. The isolate Serratia nematodiphila (MIC > 250 mM) achieved 96.18% Sb 3+ removal under Box-Behnken-optimized conditions (27.7 ℃, pH 4.67, 205.6 rpm). Time-resolved SEM-EDS, Raman, XRD, and XPS revealed a non-classical mineralization pathway from an amorphous precursor to crystalline Sb 2 O 3 within 36 h. Integrated genomic-transcriptomic-proteomic analyses resolved a coordinated physiological response: (1) energy metabolic remodeling via upregulated TCA cycle and fatty acid β-oxidation and suppressed anaerobic respiration, may help sustain NAD(P)H and proton motive force that could support ArsB-mediated efflux; (2) Fe-S cluster repair and metal sequestration through Suf assembly, iron/siderophore uptake, and molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis; (3) multi-level antioxidant defense via glutathione, catalase/peroxidase, and SoxR/OxyR systems; and (4) motility suppression, conserving energy and protons while enhanced capsule/EPS functions promote Sb adsorption and mineral nucleation. Together, these processes may promote the hydrolysis and precipitation of aqueous Sb 3+ species, leading to the formation of crystalline Sb 2 O 3 . Serratia nematodiphila orchestrates a coordinated metabolic reprogramming that enhances energy generation, metal sequestration, and oxidative defense while suppressing motility, effectively transforming toxic aqueous Sb 3+ into valuable crystalline Sb 2 O 3 . These findings provide a mechanistic blueprint for engineering microbial-based bioremediation and resource recovery from antimony-polluted environments.

title: A single-cell multimodal foundation model enables cross modality analysis between transcriptome and chromatin
authors: Bao, X.; Zhu, J.; Song, X.; et al.
abstract: Most single-cell studies measure either gene expression or chromatin accessibility, and connecting the two usually requires fitting a model to each study. Here we present MUTUAL (MUltiome Transfer in a Unified Aligned Latent space), which keeps the single-cell foundation models scFoundation and EpiAgent frozen, combines their embeddings with linear summaries of each modality and learns a shared RNA--ATAC space from 3.0 million paired cells of 400 public multiome datasets. Applied without refitting to ten datasets not used for training, MUTUAL matched cells' RNA and ATAC profiles more accurately than methods fitted on other donors of the same dataset, annotated ATAC-only cells more accurately and transferred transcription-factor motif activity to RNA-only cells beyond what cell-type assignment provides. In a maturation series of stem-cell-derived islets, motif activity predicted from RNA largely reproduced the measured stage-wise changes when other libraries of the series served as the reference. MUTUAL makes public multiome data directly usable by single-modality studies.

title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
authors: He, D.; Patro, R.; Nassar, M.; et al.
abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altoslabs/scRM.

title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals inflammatory metabolic programs in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
authors: Zhou M, Wang G, Li Y, et al.
abstract: Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by inflammatory signaling and metabolic adaptation within the tumor microenvironment. We integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets to characterize inflammation-associated metabolic programs in PDAC. Methods Three public PDAC datasets were analyzed: TCGA-PAAD bulk RNA-seq data, GSE62452 tumor and adjacent tissue microarray data, and GSE154778 single-cell RNA-seq data from primary and metastatic PDAC. Kynurenine-, arachidonic acid-, inflammasome-, and glutamine-related transcriptional modules were evaluated. Cell-based qRT-PCR was used to validate selected inflammatory-metabolic genes after 48 h of cytokine stimulation. Results In GSE62452, 5985 of 33,297 probes were differentially expressed between tumor and adjacent tissues, including 3701 increased and 2284 decreased probes. Among selected targets, KYNU showed the largest increase. In 60 matched pairs, IDO1, KYNU, PTGS2, and PLA2G4A were significantly elevated in tumor tissues. Analysis of 14,926 single cells showed that myeloid cells had the highest mean scores across all four inflammatory-metabolic modules. Bulk expression patterns were positively associated across datasets (Spearman ρ=0.745, P = 0.0133). qRT-PCR further demonstrated cytokine-induced expression of selected inflammatory-metabolic genes. Conclusions Integrated bulk and single-cell analyses identify inflammation-associated metabolic transcriptional programs in PDAC, with prominent activity in myeloid cells. These findings provide a transcriptomic framework for future mechanistic and multi-omic validation rather than direct evidence of metabolic flux or clinical utility.

title: Integrative bioinformatics and experimental validation of the prognostic and functional relevance of XDH and ITPA in non-small cell lung cancer
authors: Zhang W, Song J, Zhu H, et al.
abstract: Purine metabolism has been implicated in tumor biology and immune regulation, but the clinical and biological relevance of purine metabolism-related genes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains incompletely defined. Transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, together with TCGA clinical data, were analyzed to identify differentially expressed purine metabolism-related genes and assess their prognostic associations. Immune infiltration was evaluated using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), and single-cell transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to characterize the cellular context of candidate genes. Stemness features and drug sensitivity were assessed using transcriptome-based computational models. XDH and ITPA protein expression was examined by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry (IHC) in an independent NSCLC cohort and in cell models. Stable knockdown of XDH or ITPA was performed in H1299 cells, with key functional findings further evaluated in A549 cells. Cisplatin sensitivity was assessed using cell-viability dose-response assays in H1299 and A549 cells. Several purine metabolism-related genes were upregulated in NSCLC and associated with overall survival (OS). XDH and ITPA showed higher protein expression in tumor tissues and were associated with adverse clinicopathological features and poorer survival. Higher expression of these genes was also associated with altered immune infiltration patterns. The messenger RNA-based stemness index (mRNAsi) was associated with ITPA and XDH expression in different directions, whereas higher XDH expression was associated with higher predicted half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values for cisplatin. Knockdown of XDH or ITPA attenuated proliferative, clonogenic, migratory, and invasive phenotypes in H1299 cells, with key findings reproduced in A549 cells. XDH knockdown also reduced the experimentally determined cisplatin IC50 in both H1299 and A549 cells. XDH and ITPA may represent candidate prognostic and functionally relevant purine metabolism-related genes in NSCLC. The integrated clinical, computational, and cellular findings support their association with NSCLC progression-related phenotypes, while the underlying molecular mechanisms and broader clinical applicability require further investigation.

title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
authors: Dalal, A. K.; Lundstedt, J.; Ernecoff, N.; et al.
abstract: Background: Electronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from structured electronic health record (EHR) data may incompletely capture functional deficits. Large language models (LLMs) can extract frailty-related information from clinical notes, but whether improved frailty ascertainment improves prognostic performance is uncertain. Objective: To compare frailty ascertainment and prognostic performance between standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs among hospitalized adults. Design: Retrospective cohort study Participants: Adults aged 50 years or older enrolled in two studies at an academic medical center and affiliated community hospital between February 2022 and April 2024. Main Measures: A validated 35-deficit diagnosis-based eFI and an LLM-enhanced eFI incorporating deficits extracted from physical therapy (PT) documentation using GPT-4o. Frailty was defined using an index threshold of 0.20 or more. The primary outcome was a composite of discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations with the outcome, and discrimination was compared using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary analyses examined threshold-based classification and PT-documentation availability; prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated population and outcome restrictions. Results: Among 616 hospitalizations, mean (SD) age was 70.9 (10.2) years, 329 (53.4%) had PT documentation, and 320 (51.9%) experienced the composite outcome. Standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs classified 216 (35.1%) and 362 (58.8%) hospitalizations as frail, respectively. Both were independently associated with the outcome (standard eFI: adjusted OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.39-2.83]; LLM-enhanced eFI: adjusted OR, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.75-3.47]). Discrimination did not differ significantly (AUROC, 0.636 vs 0.660; difference, 0.024 [95% CI, -0.006 to 0.053]; p=0.12). LLM enhancement increased sensitivity (42.5% to 69.4%) but decreased specificity (73.0% to 52.7%). Conclusions: LLM enhancement substantially increased frailty ascertainment and sensitivity for adverse outcomes but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination. Thus, LLM-enhanced frailty assessment may depend on whether the intended use prioritizes broad identification of functional vulnerability or prediction of adverse post-hospital outcomes.

title: PREMISE: A Quality-Aware Probabilistic Framework for High-Resolution Source Assignment in Metagenomic Sequencing
authors: Vijendran, S.; Dorman, K.; Anderson, T. K.; et al.
abstract: Metagenomic applications, from influenza A virus (IAV) subtype tracking to bacterial strain resolution, frequently require sub-species resolution.However, traditional $k$-mer-based methods fragment reads into short $k$-mers and discard per-base quality scores.By omitting both intra-read linkage and error information, these methods confound closely related genomic variants, thereby impeding real-time pathogen surveillance and containment.We introduce \premise (Pathogen Resolution via Expectation-Maximization In Sequencing Experiments), a probabilistic, alignment-based framework implemented in Rust for high-resolution source assignment against near-complete reference databases.\premise aligns whole reads using a bidirectional run-length FM-index and quantifies reference abundances with a quality-aware Expectation-Maximization algorithm mapped over a taxonomy.This framework applies an optional sparsity penalty to resolve ambiguous assignments, which is particularly important when sparse samples are mapped against reference databases rich in highly homologous candidate references.On ten dense CAMI II strain-madness samples, \premise achieves the highest species-level read classification F1 score ($0.992$) among eight evaluated methods, with no false-positive or missed species.At the strain level, \premise maps reads to their source genome with top precision ($0.80$ vs. at most $0.64$ for competing methods), achieves 100\% recall, and estimates abundances as accurately as the best competing tool.These results demonstrate \premise's ability to provide rigorous, uncertainty-aware source resolution across both dense and sparse metagenomes, accurately resolving targets ranging from viral subtypes to bacterial strains.\\textbf{Availability:} \url{https://github.com/sriram98v/premise} under an MIT license.\\textbf{Contact:} \href{sriramv@iastate.edu}{sriramv@iastate.edu}\\

title: MintCNA: A Unified Framework for Integrative Copy Number Profiling with Single-Cell Multi-Omics Data
authors: Bao, W.; Xiao, F.
abstract: Chromosomal copy number alterations (CNAs) are key drivers of tumor evolution, disease progression and therapeutic resistance, and their identification is critical for delineating tumor clonal structure. However, accurately detecting CNAs from single-cell data remains challenging as most existing CNA callers still analyze a single omics layer and are susceptible to assay-specific noise. Recently, single-cell multi-omics techniques have enabled joint sequencing of multiple molecular layers (e.g., genomics and transcriptomics) simultaneously in the same cells, yet computational methods that fully exploit such complementary multi-omics data for CNA analysis remain limited. Here, we present MintCNA, a unified framework for CNA detection from paired single-cell multi-omics data. MintCNA integrates deep-learning based denoising with a missingness-adjusted multivariate change-point detection procedure to enhance CNA profiling across omics layers. In simulations, MintCNA outperformed existing single-cell CNA callers across all evaluated scenarios. MintCNA showed the highest correlation with bulk whole-genome sequencing in a colorectal cancer dataset and revealed progressive loss of chromosome 17 during metastasis. In an IDH-mutant glioma cohort, MintCNA generalized to paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data and identified copy number subclones corresponding to distinct malignant cell states. MintCNA provides an advanced multi-omics integrative single-cell CNA analysis tool for better delineating the mechanisms underlying disease progression and tumor evolution.

title: Cellular context shapes the transcriptomic impact of somatic variants
authors: Sun, P.; Jia, P.; Lou, C.; et al.
abstract: Somatic SNVs are commonly prioritized by recurrence or sequence annotation, leaving the molecular consequences of private variants unresolved. We developed PrismSNV and Ligo-Seq, a single-cell full-length transcriptome sequencing platform, to quantify transcriptomic displacement associated with within-cell SNV-state toggling. Across 26 samples from three cancer types, more than 60% of candidate SNVs showed significant cell-type-specific displacement with over 30% variation in magnitude. Sequence-based deleteriousness was poorly aligned with cellular displacement, and fewer than 3% of top-displacement SNVs across six tumor types were catalogued in ClinVar. Displacement was strongest in transcriptionally plastic, less differentiated states. Analysis of 655,349 CD4+ T-cell transcriptomes further showed that SNV-gene associations changed in magnitude and sometimes direction during activation. Lack of recurrence or clinical annotation does not imply transcriptomic inertness; variant impact is shaped by cellular context rather than sequence alone, establishing the variant-cell pair as a critical unit for interpreting somatic variation.

title: Variantscape: Retrospective Study of Large Language Model-Based Extraction of Variant-Treatment-Cancer Associations from Published Oncology Abstracts
authors: Wosny, M.; Blindu, A. S.; Boesch, M.; et al.
abstract: ObjectivesPrecision oncology relies on accurate interpretation of tumour-detected gene variants, to guide personalised treatment decisions. However, interpretation of variants in context requires extensive information that is often buried within unstructured biomedical literature and obscured by inconsistent nomenclature, making manual retrieval labour-intensive and prone to omissions. In this study, our aim was to evaluate the potential of large language models to extract variant-treatment-cancer associations at scale from published abstracts. DesignWe developed Variantscape, a large-scale, automated pipeline and open-access web tool. It integrates traditional natural language processing methods with state-of-the-art large language models to extract, standardise, and analyse co-associations between genetic variants, cancer types, and therapeutic interventions from published biomedical abstracts. ResultsFrom over 3.7 million abstracts published between January 2014 and October 2026, 886,195 articles containing gene names were eligible for extraction. Among these, 37,895 (4.3%) mentioned a variant, cancer type, and therapeutic agent together, covering 11,985 unique variants across 197 cancer types and 547 therapeutic agents. LLM verification against the abstract text confirmed at least one association in 35,224 papers, giving a literature-derived graph of 10,571 nodes and 44,644 verified edges. Canonical alterations in well-studied cancers (e.g., BRAF V600E in melanoma) were strongly linked to established treatments, while several rare variants also emerged with high-confidence literature support. ConclusionsBy applying large language models to biomedical literature, Variantscape enables scalable, context-aware extraction of trilateral variant-treatment-cancer relationships. This approach supports early evidence synthesis/hypothesis generation, highlights underrecognized or rare associations for MTB preparation, and offers a practical resource for accelerating discovery and supporting precision oncology research and translation. FundingThis study was funded by the School of Medicine at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland under grant number 2300380. Article SummaryO_ST_ABSStrengths and limitations of this studyC_ST_ABS[bullet] Variantscape combines traditional natural language processing with large language models to enable scalable, automated extraction of variant-cancer-treatment relationships from over 3.7 million biomedical abstracts, substantially reducing the manual search burden inherent to existing molecular tumour board workflows. [bullet]The pipeline applies large language model-based inference to standardise inconsistent genetic nomenclature across the literature, improving the comparability and reliability of extracted associations that would otherwise be obscured by terminological variation. [bullet]Variantscape is designed as a continuously updatable, open-access resource, meaning it can incorporate newly published evidence without requiring repeated manual intervention. [bullet]The pipeline relies solely on abstract-level text rather than full-text articles, which may limit the depth and granularity of extracted associations, as key methodological details, variant context, and nuanced clinical findings are frequently reported only within the body of published papers. [bullet]Automated extraction using large language models introduces a risk of misattribution of variant-cancer-treatment relationships, and without systematic manual validation of outputs, the precision of identified associations at scale remains difficult to fully characterise.

title: Benchmark of THReD: Evaluating an LLM Agent and Its Preprocessing Tools for Turning Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets
authors: Javad Mohammad Alizadeh, Huanmei Wu
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, yet little evidence shows how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether the tools they invoke give correct, reproducible output. We report a benchmark of THReD, a web-based system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat agent whose proposed steps run only after user confirmation. The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests calling for no action, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange; success is judged by checks on the produced data. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations, the deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault, and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%; goal-level requests were hardest (80.6%). Six experiments on real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and on synthetic data at scale validate the tools: 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct in masked reconstruction; a dictionary builder combining curated dictionaries with LLM suggestions mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly; all 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files under pinned dependencies; subgroup differences in inference accuracy vanished within facility and lookup key; and the same-day consolidation rule changed 90-day emergency revisit rates by up to 3.2 points without shifting cohort composition by more than one point. Processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records while the prompt stayed at about 13 thousand tokens.

title: An integrative GWAS, Transcriptomic, and domestication analysis Uncovers Multi-Layered genetic architecture of kernel rate in maize testcross hybrids
authors: Xiong X, Duan H, Ding D, et al.
abstract: Introduction Improving yield efficiency in maize (Zea mays L.) is increasingly important under high-density production systems, where gains from total biomass accumulation are approaching physiological limits. Kernel Rate (KR), or shelling percentage, captures reproductive biomass partitioning within the ear but remains less well characterized genetically than absolute yield components. Objective Here, we evaluated KR together with ear weight (EW), cob weight (CW), and kernel weight (KW) in two testcross populations generated with Mo17 and Zheng58 and assessed across six year-by-location environments. KR was highly heritable, showed only weak correlations with EW, and was consistently negatively correlated with CW, supporting its use as an index of relative kernel-to-cob biomass allocation. Methods To investigate the genetic basis of this variation, we applied an integrative analytical framework combining testcross-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS), comparative parental-line transcriptomic comparisons associated with extreme F 1 testcross performance, and population genomic signals from domestication scans. Rather than identifying a single set of causal genes, this approach revealed limited overlap among data layers, indicating that yield efficiency is shaped by multiple, context-dependent genetic contributions. Results GWAS identified multiple trait-associated loci with limited overlap across environments and tester backgrounds; two CW associations also met FDR_BH Conclusion These results support a multi-layered and context-dependent genetic basis of biomass partitioning in maize testcross hybrids. The integrative framework provides biologically informed candidate priorities for functional validation and breeding across additional testers and environments.

title: Population-scale genomics reveals divergent pathogenicity of variant classes across paralogous collagen IV genes
authors: Tzoumkas K, Doctor GT, Sadeghi-Alavijeh O, et al.
abstract: Monoallelic pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in COL4A3 and COL4A4 occur in approximately 1 in 106 individuals, yet whether these paralogous genes confer equivalent pathogenicity for the same variant classes has not been tested at population scale. Using whole-genome sequencing data from the UK Biobank (UKB; n ≈ 500,000), with replication in the All of Us Research Program (n ≈ 414,000), we performed per-variant association testing, gene-based collapsing analyses, and phenome-wide association studies (PheWASs) across hematuria, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease. We identified 64 COL4A3 and 92 COL4A4 rare variants significantly associated with hematuria or proteinuria, providing population-level quantitative evidence that may support variant interpretation. Glycine substitutions within collagenous domains conferred similar risks in both genes. In contrast, truncating and non-collagenous domain (NC1) missense variants were strongly associated with hematuria and proteinuria in COL4A4 heterozygotes but showed substantially attenuated or absent associations in COL4A3 heterozygotes despite comparable allele frequencies and predicted pathogenicity scores. These findings were independently replicated in All of Us. Genome-wide association analysis identified the COL4A3 and COL4A4 locus as the dominant genetic determinant of hematuria, attributable to the aggregate effects of rare coding variants with no evidence of independent common variant or trans-acting modifier effects. These findings demonstrate marked gene-specific differences in association with hematuria and proteinuria for truncating and NC1 variants between COL4A3 and COL4A4, challenging assumptions of equivalent pathogenicity across paralogous collagen IV genes. Gene identity, not variant class alone, should inform risk stratification, variant interpretation, and genetic counseling in collagen IV heterozygotes.

title: Integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of human cartilage reveals coordinated changes in fibronectin expression, splicing, and receptor signaling during osteoarthritis progression
authors: Lotz, M.; Swahn, H.; Sakamoto, T.; et al.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is defined by progressive loss of articular cartilage, but how chondrocytes change as the disease advances is unclear because most studies have focused on end-stage tissue. We profiled human knee articular cartilage across the full range of macroscopic OA grade, from young healthy to aged severe OA donors, by bulk RNA sequencing of 92 knees, single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 108,600 chondrocyte nuclei from 30 donors and single-nucleus multiome sequencing of 24 of these donors, treating grade as a continuous variable. With increasing grade, cartilage increased extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and remodeling genes, lost glucocorticoid-responsive, lipid-metabolic and antioxidant programs, and changed the splicing of a small set of ECM transcripts, led by the extra domain B (EDB) exon of fibronectin (FN1). Nine chondrocyte clusters were present in every disease stage and formed a continuum ordered by cartilage zone and hypertrophic differentiation, with PRG4+ superficial and COL10A1+ hypertrophic chondrocytes as the only distinct cell types at its ends and a pre-hypertrophic state between them. With grade, all clusters shared a response in which ECM production rose and homeostatic programs fell, and they differed in which of its components was strongest: ECM production in the superficial cells, the secretory pathway in the hypertrophic and CYTL1+ cells, and inflammatory signaling in the ANXA1+ and CRISPLD2+ cells. Inferred communication between chondrocytes was remodeled with stage. FN1 was induced in every cluster in excess of its fibril-assembly machinery, together with the fibronectin-cleaving protease HTRA1, and FN1 signaling shifted in receptor use from integrin 5{beta}1 toward CD44 and, less robustly, v{beta}8, accompanied by a rise in TGF-{beta}/SMAD response genes. In four early-OA donors, tenascin-C was already largely induced and the FN1 receptor shift from 5{beta}1 toward CD44 was partly present, whereas the rise of FN1 outside superficial chondrocytes, of FGF1 and of developmental and ossification programs came with progression. Chromatin accessibility changed in the same direction across clusters, with regions linked to FN1 opening and regions linked to ITGA5 closing. OA progression in human cartilage therefore appears to be a change of chondrocyte state that differs in emphasis along a zonal and hypertrophic continuum and includes changes in fibronectin regulation, production, processing, and receptor engagement.

title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions
authors: Magbanua, M. J. M.; Huppert, L. A.; Cruz, J.; et al.
abstract: BackgroundMalignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. MethodsWe applied a pre-trained deep learning model to brightfield images of single cells from malignant effusions of 10 patients with metastatic breast cancer to extract morphological features, quantify tumor cell fraction (TCF), and guide label-free microfluidic enrichment. We profiled copy-number alterations and somatic mutations in enriched tumor cell fractions and compared them with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors. ResultsAI-powered single-cell morphological analysis identified putative tumor cells in all 10 patients (median TCF, 5.4%; range, 0.51-15.8%; n = 25 samples). AI estimates of major immune-cell populations varied across patients and samples and correlated with flow cytometry measurements (n = 21 paired samples, Pearson r = 0.69-0.75). Unsupervised analysis identified four tumor cell morphotypes, revealing intra- and inter-patient morphological heterogeneity and longitudinal variation in morphotype composition. Genomic profiling of enriched tumor cell fractions by low-pass whole-genome sequencing (n = 26 samples) and whole-exome sequencing (n = 24 samples) identified copy-number alterations and somatic mutations, with tumor fraction influencing genomic signal strength. Comparisons of genomic profiles from tumor cell-enriched fractions with matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors revealed shared genomic alterations, providing orthogonal support for tumor origin and relatedness, while differences across analytes revealed genomic divergence and tumor heterogeneity. ConclusionAI-powered analysis leverages single-cell morphology for tumor cell identification and label-free enrichment, while integration with genomic profiling enables simultaneous interrogation of phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. This approach expands the potential of malignant effusions for liquid biopsy applications and biomarker development and discovery.

title: Functional Heritability Partitioning, Multi-Tissue Transcriptomic Colocalization, and Pharmacogenomic Target Deconvolution Across 127 Alzheimer's Disease Susceptibility Loci
authors: Menendez-Gonzalez, M.
abstract: Background: The landmark genome-wide association meta-analysis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD-by-proxy across N = 2,815,127 individuals (Uffelmann et al., Nature, 2026) expanded the known susceptibility landscape to 127 independent genomic risk loci (160 association signals) and established an autosomal common-variant SNP heritability of h2_SNP = 16.0% on the liability scale. Translating these 127 static statistical signals into pathway-stratified clinical trials requires resolving three quantitative gaps: how the non-APOE polygenic architecture partitions across distinct cellular programs, which effector genes operate via cortical parenchymal versus peripheral myeloid gene expression, and which targets possess nanomolar human bioactivity suitable for genetically stratified trials. Methods: Operating entirely on individual-genotype-free summary statistics structured along a previously established tridimensional diagnostic framework (Axis 1: Etiology and Genetic Architecture; Axis 2: Molecular Pathophysiology and Biomarker Programs; Axis 3: Neuroanatomical-Cognitive Topography; Menendez-Gonzalez, Alzheimers Dement, 2025), we ingested the complete NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog build GCST90695466 (8,159,496 autosomal and 160,704 X-chromosome variants). First, we performed functional heritability partitioning via stratified excess chi-square inflation and additive genetic variance (sum 2pq*beta^2) across +/-50 kb cis-regulatory windows of 50 fine-mapped effector genes organized into five mechanistic Axis 2 programs (MICROGLIAL_IMMUNE, PROTEOPATHY_AUTOPHAGY, ENDOCYTIC_VESICULAR, SYNAPTIC_CALCIUM, and MITOCHONDRIAL_OXIDATIVE). Second, we conducted Summary-data-based Mendelian Randomization (SMR) and Approximate Bayes Factor colocalization (PP.H4) across 54 human tissues in GTEx v10 (4,415 matched cis-eQTLs) alongside Open Targets v4 SuSiE fine-mapped credible sets spanning ROS/MAP dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), BrainSeq, primary human monocytes, and UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) plasma pQTLs. Third, we queried EMBL-EBI ChEMBL v34 across 2,785 human bioactivity assays (IC50, Ki, Kd, EC50) and Open Targets tractability matrices to construct an empirical pharmacogenomic target atlas. Results: Across 8,159,496 autosomal variants, the genome-wide mean test statistic was chi2_GW = 1.5099. Outside the APOE/TOMM40 super-locus (max chi2 = 3,267.15; 2pq*beta^2 = 0.0882, accounting for 74.82% of top-locus additive variance), 89,589 cis-regulatory SNPs across 48 non-APOE effector genes exhibited a 12.88-fold heritability enrichment over the autosomal background. Normalized across the 16.0% polygenic liability scale, non-APOE functional heritability concentrated in MICROGLIAL_IMMUNE (39.22% share; h2_SNP = 6.28%; 13.02x enrichment; mean chi2 = 7.64) and PROTEOPATHY_AUTOPHAGY (36.34% share; h2_SNP = 5.81%; 14.98x enrichment; mean chi2 = 8.64), followed by ENDOCYTIC_VESICULAR (16.71% share; h2_SNP = 2.67%; 12.69x enrichment; mean chi2 = 7.47), SYNAPTIC_CALCIUM (5.40% share; h2_SNP = 0.86%; 10.05x enrichment; mean chi2 = 6.13), and MITOCHONDRIAL_OXIDATIVE (2.33% share; h2_SNP = 0.37%; 5.24x enrichment; mean chi2 = 3.67). Multi-tissue SMR and colocalization resolved a striking divergence between Axis 3 cortical parenchyma and myeloid compartments: QPCT (rs2300880; Z_SMR = -4.62, p_SMR = 3.93e-6, PP.H4_cis = 0.919, PP.H4_local = 0.994 in Brain_Cortex; PP.H4_local = 0.979 in Brain_Frontal_Cortex_BA9) and AXL (rs12979764; p_SMR = 2.13e-4, PP.H4_cis = 0.902, PP.H4_local = 0.924 in Brain_Cortex) colocalized directly within human cerebral cortex and ROS/MAP DLPFC. Conversely, canonical myeloid and endocytic drivers (BIN1, CD33, TREM2, INPP5D, SYK) exhibited near-zero bulk cortical eQTL colocalization (PP.H4_cis <= 0.025 in Brain_Cortex) despite high SuSiE Locus-to-Gene scores (L2G = 0.875-0.968) and robust colocalization in primary monocytes and spleen (INPP5D PP.H4_local = 0.992; BIN1 PP.H4_local = 0.999). ChEMBL v34 bioactivity profiling confirmed low-nanomolar human target potency for clinical-stage compounds across all five programs, including isradipine (2.0 nM) and nilvadipine (19.0 nM) for CACNA1S, omaveloxolone (2.2 nM) for KEAP1, fostamatinib/R406 (41.0 nM) for SYK, and varoglutamstat/PQ912 (61.0 nM) for QPCT. Conclusion: Over three-quarters (75.56%) of the non-APOE common-variant heritability of Alzheimer's disease resides within microglial immune surveillance and proteopathic clearance networks. If prospectively validated in genotype-stratified clinical cohorts, these empirical summary-statistics findings suggest that therapeutic efficacy in sporadic AD may depend on matching pathway-selective drugs to a patient's individual Functional Pathway Burden Score rather than administering uniform monotherapies to genetically unstratified populations.

title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
authors: Liang, X.; Jayakumar, R.; Strbenac, D.; et al.
abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.

title: scCircaSim: A Circadian Simulator for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Li, C.; Zhang, L.; Zhang, Q.; et al.
abstract: Motivation: Simulated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets that capture circadian dynamics while providing known ground truth remain scarce, limiting systematic evaluation of circadian analysis methods. Results: We developed scCircaSim to generate circadian single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from a single-time-point reference. The framework combines phase progression with reference-derived network propagation of anchor gene rhythms and incorporates neighborhood effects for spatial simulation. Outputs retain reference heterogeneity and provide known cell or spot phases, rhythmicity labels, and gene-level mesor, amplitude, and phase values. Validation showed retention of reference structure and recovery of specified temporal patterns. Benchmarks of four cell phase inference methods and three rhythmic gene analysis methods revealed differences in phase accuracy, rhythmicity detection, and parameter recovery. scCircaSim supports reproducible method evaluation and preliminary experimental planning. Availability and Implementation: scCircaSim is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/Liwei-DynamicsLab/scCircaSim.

title: Pheno+: An Electronic Health Record-Integrated, Clinician-in-the-Loop Application for Efficient Phenotyping in Clinical Genomics
authors: Lebleu, E. L.; Cooperstein, I. B.; Jenkins, S. M.; et al.
abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficiency and diagnostic utility of Pheno+, an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated application that streamlines the generation of structured phenotypes for genomic testing and analysis. Materials and MethodsWe developed Pheno+ as a Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (SMART on FHIR) application embedded within the University of Utah Health EHR. Pheno+ applies ClinPhen to clinician-selected clinical notes to identify candidate Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, which clinicians review and curate within the EHR. We conducted an eight-case crossover evaluation comparing workflow time between Pheno+ and a standard workflow that involved physician chart review and molecular geneticist-led HPO term selection. In a separate cohort of 17 patients with confirmed monogenic diagnoses, we assessed the diagnostic utility of Pheno+-derived HPO terms by evaluating Exomiser gene prioritization performance using these terms. ResultsPheno+ reduced mean total workflow time by 66%, from 31.1 to 10.5 minutes (p < 0.001). Incorporating Pheno+-derived HPO terms improved Exomisers ability to rank the causative gene first, from 11 of 17 cases (64.7%) without phenotype input to 17 of 17 cases (100%) with phenotype input (p = 0.031). Discussion and ConclusionPheno+ reduced the time and personnel required to generate clinician-curated HPO term lists while producing phenotypes that improved causative gene prioritization. These findings support EHR-integrated, clinician-in-the-loop phenotyping as an efficient approach to generating diagnostically informative phenotype data for clinical genomic workflows.

title: Benchmarking DNA Foundation Models: Biological Blind Spots in Evo2 Variant-Effect Prediction
authors: Mathur, V.; Sachidanandam, R.
abstract: DNA foundation models such as Evo2 and DNABERT-2 show promise for variant-effect prediction (VEP), yet rigorous benchmarks assessing their ability to capture established biological constraints remain limited. Here, we introduce controlled benchmarks based on well-characterized nuclear and mitochondrial sequence features. Although Evo2 achieves strong aggregate performance on mitochondrial variants (AUROC = 0.927), our analyses reveal systematic blind spots in short-range signals, including codon usage bias, as well as spurious sensitivity to biologically neutral sequence context. Notably, changes in flanking sequences can cause pathogenic tRNA variants to be misclassified as benign. These findings suggest that Evo2's predictive performance may rely more heavily on learned sequence regularities than on the biological constraints governing variant function, raising concerns about the clinical utility of zero-shot genomic foundation models.Our framework provides a principled basis for standardized model evaluation and for guiding the development of architectures better aligned with biological constraints.

title: Variant Classification of a Non-Protein Coding Gene: ACMG/AMP Specifications for RMRP from the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel
authors: Jacovas, V. C.; Demirkol, Y.; Nieto-Patlan, A.; et al.
abstract: PurposeThis study, conducted by the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel (ClinGen SCID-VCEP), aimed to adapt the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) framework for germline variant interpretation in RMRP. Unlike the protein-coding genes for which the framework was primarily developed, RMRP encodes a non-protein-coding RNA. Biallelic pathogenic variants in RMRP cause cartilage-hair hypoplasia, which can include severe combined immunodeficiency disease and other immune abnormalities. MethodsAn RMRP-focused SCID-VCEP subgroup reviewed all 28 ACMG/AMP evidence criteria using population databases, published clinical and experimental data, computational predictions, and expert consensus. Each criterion was retained, modified, or designated as not applicable based on RMRP biology and disease mechanisms. The resulting specifications were pilot tested using 27 variants selected from ClinVar and research laboratory data. ResultsFifteen ACMG/AMP criteria were determined to be applicable to RMRP, while 13 were considered not applicable. Several criteria were modified to evaluate nucleotide-level effects on transcriptional regulation, critical promoter regions, and RNA secondary structure. The specifications also incorporated RMRP-specific recommendations for population frequency, functional evidence, variant phase, segregation, and phenotype. Application of the specifications classified 6 variants as pathogenic, 10 as likely pathogenic, 7 as variants of uncertain significance, and 4 as benign. Previously pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants remained within the pathogenic spectrum, and all previously benign variants remained benign. Variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations were resolved as either likely pathogenic or uncertain. PM1, PM3, and PP4 were the primary criteria supporting pathogenic classifications. ConclusionThe SCID-VCEP specifications provide a standardized approach to the classification of germline RMRP variants in cartilage-hair hypoplasia and demonstrate how the ACMG/AMP framework can be adapted for a disease-associated non-protein-coding RNA gene. These specifications support the development of variant interpretation frameworks for other clinically relevant non-protein-coding genes.

title: Global distribution of <i>CYP2C19</i> variants in clopidogrel-indicated populations: implications for pharmacogenomic-guided antiplatelet therapy
authors: Antonopoulos TC, Hughes JJ, Soueid R, et al.
abstract: Clopidogrel is a widely prescribed antiplatelet prodrug, with activation affected by CYP2C19 loss- and gain-of-function variants. Whilst global CYP2C19 variant prevalence is well described, this scoping review characterises CYP2C19 diplotype and metaboliser phenotype frequencies in clopidogrel-indicated populations. A literature search of Scopus, PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, and Ovid Embase was conducted from inception to 6 July 2026. Forty-one studies ( n = 18958) reporting CYP2C19 diplotypes were synthesised across Asia, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), Europe and the Americas and converted to phenotypes. Intermediate and poor metabolisers were most prevalent in East Asia (54.0-77.2%) and South Asia (47.3-71.1%). Rapid and ultrarapid metabolisers were most prevalent in MENA (27.3-44.3%) and Europe (27.3-36.2%). Frequent diplotypes were *1/*2 in intermediate and *2/*2 in poor metabolisers. Overall, phenotype distribution reflects global population trends. High global prevalence of CYP2C19 intermediate and poor metabolisers amongst clopidogrel-indicated populations presents an opportunity to implement pharmacogenomic-guided prescribing.

title: Integrated phenotyping, genomics, and transcriptomics reveal a constitutive drought-responsive regulatory state associated with drought adaptation in wild rice
authors: Soma F, Kawahara Y, Tanabata T, et al.
abstract: Improving drought tolerance is crucial for sustainable crop production under climate change. Identifying drought-adaptive variation in diverse genetic resources, including crop wild relatives, requires accurate and temporally resolved assessment of plant responses to water deficit. Here, we developed an indoor, unmanned phenotyping platform that can noninvasively and automatically collect temporal data on plant responses to drought stress. Using this platform, we quantified temporal drought responses in four rice cultivars and five wild rice relatives and integrated these phenotypes with chromosome-scale genome assemblies, gene annotations, and time-course transcriptomes. This integrated phenotyping, genomics, and transcriptomics identified a wild rice accession that maintained shoot growth, leaf temperature, and gene expression more stably under drought stress and exhibited a distinctive constitutive drought-responsive transcriptional state. This state included elevated basal expression of several drought-responsive genes, including ABSCISIC ACID RESPONSIVE ELEMENT-BINDING FACTOR 1 (ABF1), a known regulator of ABA-mediated drought responses. Validation using transgenic and introgression lines suggested that low-level constitutive ABF1 expression, as a component of this drought-responsive regulatory state, can improve drought performance without obvious growth penalties. These findings demonstrate the utility of automated temporal phenotyping combined with accession-specific genomic and transcriptomic resources for uncovering drought-adaptive variation in wild rice, and provide a framework for exploiting natural regulatory variation to improve drought resilience in cultivated rice.

title: An end-to-end in silico framework for truth-based validation and regression testing of clinical genome sequencing pipelines, from simulated reads to reportable findings
authors: Dvorsky, B.; Komarkova, M.; Kollinova, K.; et al.
abstract: Clinical genome sequencing pipelines change often, and each change requires proportionate revalidation. Guidelines accept in silico data as a supplement but leave variant interpretation outside pipeline validation, and, to our knowledge, no framework tests a pipeline against a known truth up to the reportable finding, so report specificity is not measured. We present a source-available framework that tests a pipeline end to end, from sequencing reads to the report, against a truth fixed before any run. It plants expert-curated pathogenic and benign variants from the same genes, and optionally synthetic variants that no database holds, into the GIAB HG002 germline background and records the expected class and report decision of each variant. It then simulates reads and runs secondary and tertiary analysis as black boxes through exchangeable adapters. Findings are compared with the truth at the call-set and report levels, each failure is assigned to the first pipeline stage where it appears, and a variant-by-variant comparison of two runs serves as a regression test. We applied the framework to nf-core/sarek with DeepVariant and to the ACMG/AMP classifier BIAS-2015, using 243 ClinGen-curated variants in five test sets. Single-nucleotide variant recall against the HG002 benchmark was 99.5% on simulated and 99.3% on real reads, and every planted variant was present in the reads and called with the correct genotype. The report included 115 of 117 pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants (98.3%) but withheld only 106 of 126 variants that must not be reported (84.1%), mainly because variants of uncertain significance were upgraded and recessive carriers were reported. Without ClinVar-derived criteria, report sensitivity fell to 74.4%. Most false reports of one test set came from diploid calling of the male chromosome X, and haploid calling removed them without side effects. In supplementary experiments, indels were called completely up to 20 bp, and BIAS-2015 left 74% of synthetic loss-of-function variants unreported because it combined criteria by the 2015 rules. The framework measures report-level sensitivity and specificity and localizes regressions, so it can supplement validation on human samples and support change control.

title: LRCQ: phenome-wide heritability enrichment of genomic loci from GWAS summary statistics
authors: Chen, L. G.; Sham, P. C.
abstract: Some genetic variants are associated with many traits, but a variant's GWAS statistics are also inflated by the effects of variants in LD with it and by confounding shared by all variants in a study. Existing measures of per-variant pleiotropy, such as counts of significant associations or multi-trait association tests, do not separate these sources. Stratified LD score regression separates them for one trait at a time and only through predefined annotations. We present LRCQ (LD score regression on {chi}2 across many GWAS), which estimates for each locus its phenome-wide heritability enrichment: the variance of its causal effects across a set of traits, relative to an average locus. LRCQ regresses squared Z-scores from 30 or more GWAS jointly on squared LD, with per-trait LDSC intercepts and heritabilities fitted in earlier stages. Its pooled least-squares solution has a closed form whose cost does not grow with the number of traits. Its standard errors account for sample overlap and genetic correlation between GWAS. Squared Z-scores identify enrichment at the resolution of LD clumps, not single SNPs, so LRCQ reports clump-level estimates ("omni-loci"). These estimates can be aggregated over any functional annotation or gene set chosen after the analysis. In simulations with real UK Biobank LD and 30 to 1,000 traits, LRCQ was unbiased for its clump-level estimand. When GWAS share samples its test statistics are strongly right-skewed: normal-reference p-values were up to 10-fold anti-conservative at P < 0.001, and skewness-corrected p-values from the exact third cumulant restored type-I error and FDR control. Model-based standard errors were calibrated once the enrichment estimates plugged into them kept the polygenic background. It ranked enriched loci better than mean {chi}2, LD-normalised {chi}2, multi-trait omnibus tests and significant-association counts in 13 of 16 scenarios. Its main vulnerability was a misspecified LDSC intercept. Applied to 444 Pan-UK Biobank European-ancestry GWAS, LRCQ found strongly non-uniform phenome-wide enrichment: the SD of true clump-mean enrichment was 8.3, against a genome mean of 1. It identified 70 omni-loci (99 LD clumps) at FDR 5%, including CRP, CETP, APOB, AKTIP, SMOX, the SHBG region, CASZ1 and HNF1A. These ranked only moderately with mean {chi}2 and poorly with counts of significant associations. Gene-level phenome-wide enrichment rose with loss-of-function constraint. Phenome-wide heritability was 3-5-fold enriched in coding, conserved, 5' UTR and promoter sequence, and depleted in repressed chromatin. LRCQ turns hundreds of biobank GWAS into an LD-corrected map of where phenome-wide genetic variance lies, and complements its companion method LRCP, which estimates genetic-effect correlations between loci.

title: gcat, its_a_scam: modular tools for single cell data processing and per-cellquality control
authors: Prabakar, R. K.; Meyer, H. V.
abstract: Motivation: The era of designing bioinformatic pipelines using open source tools is giving way to monolithic, and often proprietary, tools designed for end-to-end analysis, especially in the context of single cell data. While these tools are convenient for going from sequencing data to an almost complete data analysis "in a few clicks", they can strongly limit data use beyond standard analyses Results: We developed Gene and Chromosome Analysis Toolkit (gcat) and It's a scam To Sell Another Single Cell Analysis Method (its_a_scam) for modular processing and quality control of single cell genomic data, freeing users from their reliance on proprietary tools. gcat is a C++ library for parsing genomic data and working with it over genomic coordinates. its_a_scam is built on top of gcat and provides a suite of tools for a wide range of single cell data processing and quality control. its_a_scam can be used in conjunction with commonly used open source tools for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq count matrix generation, and for performing per-cell quality control directly from alignment files. These alignment-level per-cell metrics can be used for quality control of each cell or to understand celltype differences post-clustering or post-annotation. Using a peripheral blood mononuclear cell Multiome dataset, we show that the count matrices generated with the aid of its_a_scam are highly concordant with those generated by proprietary pipelines. The alignment metrics further demonstrate celltype differences in aligned genomic regions, metagene profiles, and genebody coverage. The modular nature of its_a_scam allows users to integrate it into their existing pipelines, while also enabling analysis beyond current pipelines. Availability: gcat (distributed as gcatlib) and its_a_scam are open source and available at https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/gcatlib and https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/its_a_scam. Detailed documentation is available at https://gcatlib.readthedocs.io/ and https://its-a-scam.readthedocs.io.

title: A population-based resource for the prioritization of rare variants of unknown significance in clinical genomics
authors: Tremblay, S.; Moreau, C.; Morin, G.-P.; et al.
abstract: Rare diseases represent a major public health challenge because they are often associated with severe phenotypes, yet many causal variants remain undiscovered. Founder populations provide a unique opportunity to identify disease-causing variants through the local enrichment of rare alleles. Using whole-genome sequencing data from individuals in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean population, enriched variants were identified and their founder status was assessed through identity-by-descent sharing. Variant impact was evaluated using functional prediction tools without relying on prior clinical classification. A total of 131 founder variants of interest were identified, most of which would likely have been overlooked by conventional approaches based on existing clinical annotations. We developed a web-based platform that facilitates clinician access to the latest interpretation of their genetic variants of interest. These findings demonstrate that potentially pathogenic variants can remain undetected even in extensively studied founder populations. More broadly, they highlight the value of population structure-based approaches for uncovering rare disease variants and improving the characterization of genetic disease risk across human populations.

title: Single-Cell Transcriptome-Wide Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analysis Reveals Immune Cell-Specific Mechanisms in Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Si, Y.; Si, Y.
abstract: Objective: To integrate single-cell expression quantitative trait locus (sc-eQTL), Alzheimer's disease (AD) genome-wide association study (GWAS), and Bayesian colocalization analyses, in order to systematically identify candidate causal genes and potential immune mechanisms that specifically regulate AD risk in peripheral immune cells. Methods: Using the cis-eQTLs of 14 peripheral blood immune cell types from the OneK1K single-cell eQTL dataset as exposure data and the AD GWAS (GCST90565439) as outcome data, a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was performed. Weak instrumental variables were removed using F-statistics, and approximately independent genetic instruments were obtained by linkage disequilibrium pruning. For significant gene-cell type associations, compareCluster functional enrichment, Bayesian colocalization, and phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) were further performed, and the 1M-scBloodNL dataset was used for replication validation. Results: The MR analysis identified 187 gene-cell type associations significantly associated with AD risk, involving 161 candidate causal genes. Among them, 141 genes showed significant associations in only a single immune cell type, suggesting that AD-related immune genetic regulation has marked cell type specificity. Functional enrichment analysis showed that the significant genes in different immune cell types were enriched in biological processes including MHC class II antigen presentation, phagocytosis, membrane invagination, and positive regulation of T cell activation. Colocalization analysis indicated a strong shared genetic signal between TNF expression in CD4+SOX4+ T cells and AD risk (PP.H4 = 0.833). In the 1M-scBloodNL replication analysis, several candidate genes showed consistent direction and nominal significance. The PheWAS results suggested that the significant phenotypic associations of the TNF instrumental variable were mainly concentrated in immune- and hematology-related traits, with no genome-wide significant neurological phenotypic associations observed. Conclusion: This study suggests that single-cell eQTL-MR combined with colocalization analysis can be used to dissect the cell type-specific genetic regulatory mechanisms of peripheral immunity in AD. The genetically predicted expression of TNF in CD4+SOX4+ T cells may represent an important immune-related signal for AD risk, but further validation in independent populations and functional experiments is still required.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Kheirolah Rahsepar Fard, Tahereh Jeirani
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks
authors: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have been reported to read, edit and write the weights of small neural networks, raising the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. Public demonstrations, however, mixed reading raw weights with running code. We separated these conditions in internally pre-specified simulation experiments. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated cohorts of patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage, each with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts under a default or an explicit system instruction, either with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool that exposed the weights (white box) or only the network's predictions (black box). Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks as unidentifiable; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box access performed as well as white-box access, and other GPT-6 models read as accurately. A well-designed script matched the comparator models on the audit and the best LLM repair. For auditing these networks, what mattered was computation and elicitation, not access to the weights.

title: Epigenome-informed Polymer Modeling Reveals Chromosome Folding Landscapes across Distinct Genetic and Epigenetic Contexts
authors: Bazmi, S.; Turco, A.; Kumar, S.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is critical for gene regulation, enabling long-range interactions between genes and distal regulatory elements. Genomic structural variations and epigenetic differences can perturb this organization, contributing to phenotypic variation and tissue-specific gene regulation. Prior studies have assessed the impact of these genetic and epigenetic changes on 3D genome folding, primarily using population-averaged features such as topologically associating domains and loops. However, growing evidence from single-cell and live-imaging studies indicates that chromosomes are highly dynamic and exist as heterogeneous ensembles of conformations. Here, we applied an epigenetic-state-informed polymer modeling framework to generate chromosomal conformational ensembles directly from cell- and tissue-specific epigenomic data. The resulting ensembles reproduced experimental Hi-C maps across cell lines and tissue types. Comparison of these conformational ensembles revealed that, although polymer dynamics were conserved across cell lines, their folding landscapes diverged. These differences arose primarily from cell-line-specific chromatin-state interaction networks and were concentrated in rare, long-lived contacts. Furthermore, modeling a TAD-boundary-disrupting deletion without re-optimizing the model parameters indicated a shift in the chromatin conformational ensemble from predominantly insulated to predominantly fused states. The modeled deletion also selectively strengthened active chromatin contacts and differentially disrupted enhancer contacts involving neighboring genes. Finally, comparison of two tissue types from the same donor revealed epigenetically driven rewiring of chromatin-state interaction networks. These findings establish chromosomal conformational ensembles as a sensitive readout of genome reorganization across distinct genetic and epigenetic contexts.

title: Single-Cell Transcriptomics Reveals Tumorigenic Lineages and Interactions Persisting and Evolving From Premalignancy to Cancer in the Stomach
authors: Vazquez, E. N.; Lozano, C. C.; Sun, X.; et al.
abstract: Background & Aims Gastric cancer is often diagnosed at advanced stages, making the premalignant window critical for early detection. However, the epithelial changes that characterize this stage remain poorly defined. We used CTLA4-knockdown (CTLA4KD) mice, which model human CTLA4 insufficiency-associated gastric cancer, that develops autoimmune gastritis, metaplasia, and adenocarcinoma, to define molecular changes across disease progression. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing and 40-color spectral flow cytometry were performed on gastric tissue across premalignant and cancer stages. We evaluated epithelial lineage relationships, cell-cell communication pathways, and candidate markers at the transcript and protein levels in murine and human gastric adenocarcinoma. Results We identified a metaplastic/tumorigenic population in CTLA4KD mice that emerged in premalignancy with a chief cell transcriptomic origin. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed a progressive increase in fibronectin (FN1) signaling from premalignancy through cancer, transitioning from stromal to autocrine signaling in the metaplastic/tumorigenic population. Expression of Embigin (EMB), a fibronectin receptor, increased at both transcript and protein levels in premalignancy and remained elevated in cancer. EMB epithelial cells co-expressed CD133, a cancer stem cell marker, consistent with a stem-like phenotype. EMB expression was also higher in human gastric adenocarcinoma than in matched normal tissue. Conclusions Using a model that captures the full histopathological cascade of gastric tumorigenesis, we delineate single-cell transcriptional programs that persist and evolve from premalignancy to adenocarcinoma. In-depth computational analyses identified novel markers involved in cell-cell communication during tumorigenesis, including EMB, an epithelial marker that persists from premalignancy through cancer in the murine model and validated in human gastric adenocarcinoma, suggesting EMB as a marker of premalignant progression.

title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
authors: Behrens, C.; Chatterjee, M.; Jernigan, C. M.; et al.
abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

title: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
authors: Pugalenthi, L. S.; Nanduri, R.; Hong, R.; et al.
abstract: Background. Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

title: Beyond a single threshold: calibration of CADD v1.7 and AlphaGenome for ACMG/AMP computational evidence across variant classes, model versions, and reference data
authors: Miranda, J. P.; Carvajal, L.; Aldana, I.; et al.
abstract: Clinical laboratories use computational predictors as supporting evidence for or against pathogenicity under the ACMG/AMP guidelines, but this evidence is reliable only when score thresholds are calibrated. Genome-wide predictors such as CADD are often applied using a single cutoff across all variant types and model versions, and the new AlphaGenome Variant Impact score (AVI) has not been calibrated. Following a prespecified plan and the ClinGen calibration method, we calibrated CADD v1.7 and AVI on rare ClinVar missense variants. Both predictors provided moderate evidence of pathogenicity and strong evidence of benignity, and their thresholds held for variants classified after calibration. AVI performed better than CADD in each comparison and approached the missense-specific predictors. Thresholds available in 2024 gave AVI evidence in the final direction for 72.5% of the variants of uncertain significance (VUS) resolved by 2026, compared with 60.5% for CADD. Applied to 1.2 million current missense VUS, the calibrated predictors agreed on pathogenic or benign evidence for four in ten, and on strong pathogenic evidence for 186 VUS reviewed by expert panels, which can be reassessed first. Outside missense variants, the same thresholds failed, producing false-benign evidence for pathogenic noncoding variants. A change in CADD version altered the evidence level for a third of variants without improving discrimination. Our results suggest that computational evidence is most reliable within the variant class and model version in which it was calibrated. In practice, laboratories may prioritize missense-specific predictors, use AVI when a genome-wide predictor is needed, and reassess thresholds after model updates.

title: Pangenome Graph Node-Phenotype Association shows GWAS-like quality results with only few individuals
authors: Carrette, C.; Sabot, F.; Muller, C.
abstract: Purpose: We introduce GraNPA (Graph Node-Phenotype Association), a method that performs a phenotype-sequence association analysis on a pangenome vari- ation graph (PVG). This PVG is built using a small number of individual genome sequences and does not require additional population materials or kinship information for qualitative phenotypes. This approach minimizes the number of individuals required for association studies and mitigates the impact of reference bias in variant calling within these types of analyses. Background: A PVG is a representation of the multiple alignment of a set of complete genomes. It contains all variations, ranging from single nucleotide poly- morphisms (SNPs) to large structural variations (SVs), and these are represented as nodes in the graph.
