By integrating phenotype information within these nodes, we can assign a Score (S ) to each one and identify regions related to the phe- notype directly within the PVG. These regions represent statistically significant shifts in S distribution, indicating their involvement in the phenotype. Finally, GraNPA provides their positions and scores for further analysis. Results: This method was tested using different simulated contexts and two publicly available datasets: the Sub1A gene locus for Asian rice Oryza sativa in a 13 individuals PVG, and the insertion responsible for the white-headed in cattle (Bos taurus) with a PVG of 24 individuals. Source code of GraNPA is available here https://forge.ird.fr/diade/graphgwas/granpa under GNU GPLv3. Conclusion: GraNPA was able to identify the expected area in two simulated datasets, as well as the loci responsible for these two known traits, using only a few dozen complete genomes from these PVGs. Although this method is currently limited to qualitative phenotypes, it paves the way for more efficient methods that rely on PVGs and a small number of individuals.

title: Prefrontal cortex transcriptomes distinguish Alzheimers disease from asymptomatic amyloid pathology, neuropeptide loss, immune-complement activation and glial remodelling
authors: Munir, Y. A.; Sagir, U.; Sajjad, F.; et al.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now defined biologically by cortical amyloid-{beta} (A) and tau (T) pathology, yet the transcriptional programmes that separate symptomatic AD (A+T+) from amyloid-positive, tau-negative pathology ageing (A+T-) and from pathology-free controls (A-T-) remain incompletely resolved in the association cortex. We re-analysed bulk RNA-sequencing data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of 15 donors (BioProject PRJNA1017546; 87 sequencing runs aggregated to donor level): Normal (n = 2), pathology ageing (n = 5) and AD (n = 8). Differential expression was tested with DESeq2 (adjusted P < 0.05, |log2 fold change| > 1), and up- and down-regulated gene sets were analysed separately by Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG over-representation. APOE and TREM2 p.Arg47His contrasts were treated as exploratory. AD versus Normal yielded 341 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 223 up, 118 down) and AD versus pathology ageing yielded 496 (358 up, 138 down), whereas pathology ageing versus Normal yielded only six. Genes reduced in AD were dominated by neuropeptide and hormone signalling (VGF, VIP, CRH, GRP, TAC1, PENK; neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, adjusted P = 8.8 x 10-5; neuropeptide hormone activity, adjusted P = 6.3 x 10-8), most of which also differed from pathology ageing. Genes increased in AD were enriched for interferon-{gamma} response, myeloid activation, adaptive immunity and classical complement (C1QA, C1QB, C1QC). Relative to pathology ageing, AD additionally showed induction of gliogenesis, oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination programmes (gliogenesis, 21 genes, adjusted P = 2.6 x 10-6; SOX10, MYRF) and of the microglial purinergic receptor gene P2RX7 (log2FC = 1.46, adjusted P = 1.5 x 10-5). All six pathology-ageing DEGs, including the myeloid genes VSIG4 and CD163, were also DEGs in AD, and 50 DEGs shared by the two AD contrasts moved in the same direction. Genotype-stratified analyses were underpowered or confounded with diagnosis. In the DLPFC, AD is therefore characterised by a graded loss of neuropeptidergic signalling, myeloid-complement activation that begins at the pathology-ageing stage, and an AD-specific glial/oligodendrocyte response. These signatures nominate candidate biomarkers and mechanisms for early intervention, but the small cohort demands replication in larger, covariate-annotated datasets.

title: CMVAE: Contrastive Supervision Improves Single-Omic Latent Manifold for Breast Cancer Survival Prognosis
authors: Singh, A.; Kohut, A.; Templeton, J. M.; et al.
abstract: High-dimensional omics data are vital for fore- casting patient prognosis in oncology. While deep multi-omics learning methods are increasingly popular, they suffer from data missingness and low patient overlap across modalities. Consequently, advancing single-omic representation learning re- mains a critical yet challenging research problem. Standard generative dimensionality reduction methods rely on recon- struction objectives that optimize the global manifold topology; however, overlook downstream clinical outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce a Contrastive Masked Denois- ing Variational Autoencoder (CMVAE), a self-supervised dual- optimization framework designed to map single-omic information into a clinical outcome-aware latent space. A stochastic feature masking strategy corrupts the input omic profiles, and CMVAE is optimized to simultaneously infer missing molecular data and contrastive alignment of patient survival trajectories. We evaluate CMVAE using leak-proof five-fold stratified cross-validation on the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort. The method outperforms traditional unsupervised methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.7397 {+/-} 0.0239 on patient prognosis. Further analysis demonstrates a highly significant (p < 0.0001) risk stratification among low vs. high risk groups. Beyond comparing within single-omic methods, CMVAE outperforms six state-of- the-art multi-omics survival baselines by a minimum of 3%. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/CMVAE. Note: Accepted at the IEEE BIBM 2026 workshop RLPD-Bio (Representation Learning and Pattern Discovery for Bioinformatics and Biomedicine).

title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
authors: Ramakrishna, P.; Strand, J.; Song, S.; et al.
abstract: PurposeTo compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). DesignRetrospective benchmarking study. Subjects4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. MethodsNine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome MeasuresDisease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. ResultsFor retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. ConclusionsOpen-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

title: El Agente Fármaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
authors: Marcel Müller, Mohammad Ghazi Vakili, Yoshihiro Ogura, et al.
abstract: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente Fármaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subsequent steps to the target and the user's objectives. Our approach centers on a shared scientific memory: Fármaco Atlas, which stores molecules, structures, and results together with their provenance -- a record of how they were obtained. The agent uses targeted database queries to retrieve the evidence needed for each decision. A single request can launch calculations for an entire collection of molecules, without requiring a separate LLM decision for every compound. This design limits the information the model must process as screening collections grow, while keeping the underlying results available for inspection and further analysis. The integrated tools support molecule generation, prediction of binding and molecular properties, and searches for compounds available for purchase. In a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign, the agent proposed chemically distinct candidates with competitive docking scores and higher calculated drug-likeness under explicitly imposed selection criteria. In a 22-task benchmark against plain tool calls and Codex, the agent achieved the highest observed mean model-judged score, with lower median cumulative token use and peak context. Fármaco provides a foundation for flexible, scalable drug discovery workflows that connect scientific reasoning with an enduring, traceable record of computational work.

title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
authors: Farnoush Rezaei Jafari, Tristan Lazard, Kenza Bouzid, et al.
abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

title: RNAactDrug 2.0: an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets
authors: Li F, Pei L, Xing J, et al.
abstract: RNAactDrug 2.0 (available at https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug or https://bio-datamining.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug) is an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets. We have updated the RNAactDrug 2.0 database with significantly expanded data and improved features, including (i) ∼30 000 drugs, 38 908 RNA molecules, and 22 800 375 drug-RNA associations from large-scale pharmacogenomic databases, covering four molecular layers: expression, copy number variation (CNV), mutation, and methylation; (ii) 11 099 cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas across 33 cancer types are integrated to support clinical and pan-cancer analyses of drug sensitivity-associated RNA features; (iii) ∼3.8 million cells from >200 single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, spanning 34 cancer types and 38 tissues, enable analysis of cell type-specific patterns and intratumoral heterogeneity; (iv) 26 440 enhancers and 788 444 drug-enhancer associations, combined with potential target prediction, provide an exploratory epigenetic regulatory dimension; (v) enhanced search and browsing functionalities, together with seven tools for functional annotation, pan-cancer analysis, tumor microenvironment profiling, single-cell trajectory and CNV analysis, and enhancer-related analyses. In summary, RNAactDrug 2.0 is a crucial resource for the multi-omics dissection of drug sensitivity-associated molecules, providing important support for the discovery of drug resistance biomarkers and the advancement of personalized therapeutic strategies.

title: Cyclotides from Clitoria ternatea: Genomic Organization, Biosynthesis, and Roles in Plant Defense
authors: Kumar R, Yeo LM, Singaram N, et al.
abstract: Clitoria ternatea, commonly known as butterfly pea, is a perennial legume widely recognized for its ornamental and medicinal value. Beyond its characteristic anthocyanin-rich blue flowers, the plant produces cyclotides, a type of ultra-stable, cyclic cystine-knot peptide, with exceptional biological functions. Unlike other cyclotide-bearing families that carry independent cyclotide genes, C. ternatea integrates cyclotide domains into albumin-1 genes, replacing β-chain domains through divergent or convergent evolution. Genomic and transcriptomic studies reveal a large repertoire of albumin-1 loci and associated biosynthetic enzymes, including asparaginyl endopeptidases (butelase-1), protein disulphide isomerases, and peptidyl-prolyl isomerases, which orchestrate the cyclization, folding, and stabilization of cyclotides. Transcriptome analyses further demonstrate tissue-specific expression patterns, with distinct cyclotides such as cliotides T2 and T3 enriched in flowers and pods, and cliotides T8-T10 specialized in seeds, reflecting adaptive responses to localized biotic stress. Functionally, C. ternatea cyclotides exhibit broad-spectrum defense properties, including insecticidal, bactericidal, nematicidal, and antifungal activities, primarily through membrane permeabilization and disruption of lipid bilayers. Their preferential affinity for phosphatidylethanolamine-rich membranes highlights their selective toxicity toward insect and microbial targets. Recent advances in synthetic biology exploit cyclotides' structural stability as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic peptide design, with applications in immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer drug development. This review consolidates genomic, transcriptomic, and functional insights into cyclotide biosynthesis and activity in C. ternatea, highlighting its evolutionary distinctiveness and biotechnological potential. Future research integrating multi-omics and spatial single-cell analyses can further unravel regulatory networks, defense dynamics, and translational applications of these unique plant peptides.

title: Integrative single cell and machine learning analysis identifies fibroblast centric hub genes and therapeutic candidates in lung adenocarcinoma and ischemic cardiomyopathy
authors: Pu Z, Liu Z, Zhang H, et al.
abstract: Background Ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) are distinct diseases but may share fibroblast mediated mechanisms involving tissue remodeling and inflammation. However, their common molecular features at single cell resolution remain insufficiently defined. Methods We integrated single cell RNA sequencing datasets from ICM and LUAD with bulk transcriptomic profiles from TCGA LUAD, GSE18842, and GSE48166. Differential expression analysis identified 36 shared core genes. A total of 127 combinations of machine learning algorithms and feature selection methods were benchmarked to identify six hub genes: KRTCAP3, RUNX2, DBF4B, C11orf80, COL3A1, and ZFP64. UCell, scMetabolism, SCISSOR, Monocle 3, CellChat, scTenifoldNet/scTenifoldKnk, virtual drug screening, and molecular docking were used for functional characterization. Results Fibroblasts were the dominant cellular source of the six hub genes in both ICM and LUAD. COL3A1 progressively increased along fibroblast pseudotime trajectories. Virtual overexpression and knockout analyses showed convergence on extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory response, and immune regulation. Cell communication analysis identified fibroblasts as major senders of COLLAGEN signaling, with recipient cells shifting from inflammatory monocytes under normal conditions to proliferating macrophages in ICM and tumor cells in LUAD. Molecular docking nominated Digoxin, Ergotamine, and Ledipasvir as candidate RUNX2-binding compounds with favorable predicted docking scores. Conclusions This study provides a single cell framework linking ICM and LUAD through fibroblast driven extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammation, and identifies potential molecular targets and therapeutic candidates for further validation.

title: Genomic landscape of ERBB3 alterations in metastatic solid tumours: a real-world data analysis
authors: Kwon M, Go Y, Shin JE, et al.
abstract: Background Although human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (ERBB2/HER2) is a validated therapeutic target, the significance of ERBB3 (HER3) alterations across solid tumours remains poorly defined. We characterised such alterations to clarify the genomic landscape relevant to HER3-directed strategies, distinguishing somatic events from germline polymorphisms. Patients and methods We analysed real-world data from 5416 patients with metastatic solid tumours who underwent next-generation sequencing. As tumour-only sequencing cannot separate germline from somatic variants, recurrent germline-pattern variants were reclassified using gnomAD and Korean population databases, and remaining somatic variants were annotated for oncogenicity using OncoKB (v7.3, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY). Overall survival (OS) was analysed via Cox regression analysis stratified according to tumour type. Results ERBB3 alterations were initially identified in 12.9% of patients, dominated by mutations (12.3%) rather than amplifications (0.8%). However, the two most common variants, K498I and R1127H, proved to be common germline polymorphisms, and germline-pattern variants accounted for 63% of all mutation calls. After germline exclusion, the prevalence of somatic mutations was 4.5%, and oncogenic/likely-oncogenic mutations only 1.6%, matching a large pan-cancer series. Oncogenic mutations clustered in extracellular domains, were tumour-type-specific (V104M/L in colorectal and urothelial; G284R in gastric and biliary tract cancer), and persisted in nonhypermutated tumours. The ERBB3 mutation status was not prognostic (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.97, P = 0.52), whereas ERBB3 amplification was independently associated with a worse OS (HR 1.43, P = 0.024). Conclusions Most apparent ERBB3 mutations in this East Asian tumour-only cohort were likely germline polymorphisms; true somatic oncogenic mutations were uncommon and tumour-type-specific, whereas amplification was rare but prognostically adverse. As HER3-directed antibody-drug conjugates depend on HER3 protein expression, the integration of such data with HER3 immunohistochemistry and outcomes is essential to define the target population.

title: Roadmap for inferring metabolic regulation using multiomics, machine learning, and genome-scale modeling
authors: Schildcrout R, Rhoads N, Chandrasekaran S
abstract: Machine learning and genome-scale metabolic modeling have accelerated the discovery of metabolic-regulatory relationships in model microbes and mammalian cells. This review provides a roadmap for integrating omics with computational methods for studying systems-level transcriptional, post-translational, and allosteric regulation. Developing methods to infer and integrate multiple regulatory mechanisms simultaneously is essential for discovering novel modes of metabolic regulation and precise engineering of metabolic networks.

title: The Reasoning Paradox in Scientific Sandboxes: Why Extended Reasoning Fails in Autonomous Bioinformatics and How to Fix It.
authors: Salami, R. O.; Amuna, D.; Akorful, R. A.; et al.
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) trained with extended reasoning, such as DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1, have established state-of-the-art benchmarks in formal logic, competitive programming, and mathematics. In interactive, empirical scientific sandboxes, however, their efficacy remains counter-intuitive. In the Bioinformatics Benchmark (BixBench), extended reasoning models paradoxically degraded in multi-turn environments, leading benchmark authors to exclude them from primary agentic evaluations. In this paper, we conduct the first systematic forensic audit of the internal cognitive monologue (<think> ... </think>) of open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) and matched instruction-tuned controls (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) deployed inside containerized computational biology sandboxes on Nvidia H100 GPUs. Our forensic analysis uncovers two distinct systemic failure modes: (1) The PubMed Prior Trap, in which reasoning models engage in epistemic rationalization within their cognitive stream, falsely convincing themselves that empirical datasets are missing and substituting empirical computation with speculative literature recall (e.g., estimating adjusted p-values based on "typical experimental outcomes"); and (2) Tag Language Nesting Collisions, in which models conflate agent-level XML action tags with Python syntax, producing terminal interpreter syntax errors. To resolve this paradox, we introduce Dual Track Decoupled Reasoning (DTDR), an agent scaffolding architecture that evicts internal cognitive monologues from multi-turn history, injects strict empirical grounding guardrails, and dynamically intercepts runtime tool invocations. On a stratified diagnostic benchmark spanning single-cell RNA-seq, bulk differential expression (DESeq2), and genomic variant prioritization (n=22 per arm), DTDR rescues the 14B reasoning model from 0.0% to 9.09% accuracy (2/22), doubling the performance of the matched non-reasoning coder control (4.55%, 1/22) while slashing code execution errors by 81% (13.6% vs. 72.7%) and reducing average steps to solution by 66% (1.77 vs. 5.18 steps). All replication pipelines, prompts, and trajectory manifests are openly released.

title: AdaGeneBudget: Cell-Adaptive Gene-Token Allocation for Efficient Single-Cell Foundation Models
authors: Kim, D.; Hwang, U.
abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) represent each cell using sequences of gene-associated tokens, making embedding extraction increasingly costly as the number of cells and expressed genes grows. Existing input policies typically rely on fixed input budgets, with retained genes determined by random subsampling, model-native ranking, or a dataset-level highly variable gene (HVG) panel. However, they do not jointly determine, for each cell, which genes to retain and how many tokens to allocate. We introduce AdaGeneBudget, a training-free gene-token selection method that combines each gene's expression with reference-derived inverse detection frequency and retains the shortest ranked prefix that captures a target fraction of the cell's expression-specificity score mass. The resulting cell-specific budget is bounded by minimum and maximum lengths, requires no cell-type labels, and leaves the pretrained backbone unchanged. We evaluated AdaGeneBudget in a frozen-backbone inference setting using pretrained scGPT and Geneformer models on Kang and PBMC reference-mapping tasks, with an additional scPRINT comparison against its official HVG policy and an expressed-only HVG control. Across four scGPT and Geneformer backbone-dataset pairs, AdaGeneBudget substantially reduced mean gene-token counts and peak GPU memory while increasing embedding-extraction throughput by up to 4.63x. Despite this compression, it preserved native-level aggregate annotation utility and numerically outperformed token-matched random and Top-Expression baselines. AdaGeneBudget also preserved fine-grained and low-support cell identities and retained lineage-marker programs and stimulation-associated pathway genes under compression. In scPRINT, both HVG controls achieved higher annotation macro-F1, whereas AdaGeneBudget more faithfully preserved the stimulation-induced embedding direction. These results establish biologically informed, cell-adaptive gene-token allocation as a practical complement to architectural and systems-level efficiency methods for applying existing scFMs to new datasets. They also suggest that cell-adaptive input allocation may be a useful design principle for future models operating under finite token budgets.

title: De Novo transcriptome assembly and functional annotation in non-model organisms
authors: Habib N, Rfaki A, Al Idrissi N, et al.
abstract: Advances in RNA sequencing have established transcriptomics as a key approach for investigating gene expression, regulation, and functional diversity across both model and non-model organisms. In the absence of high-quality reference genomes, de novo transcriptome assembly remains essential, yet its accuracy and reproducibility depend heavily on the choice and integration of computational strategies. This review provides a comprehensive and structured framework for de novo transcriptome reconstruction and functional annotation in non-model systems, integrating current best practices across quality control, assembly, redundancy reduction, and annotation workflows. We systematically compare short-read, long-read, and hybrid assembly approaches, and evaluate multi-layered annotation strategies combining homology-based, domain-based, and ontology-driven methods. We further highlight emerging developments, including long-read transcriptomics, machine learning-assisted annotation, orthology inference, and multi-omics integration, which improve transcriptome completeness and biological interpretability. Key limitations in current workflows are critically examined, including database biases, incomplete annotations, and challenges in isoform resolution, particularly in underrepresented taxa. By consolidating methodological advances with practical recommendations, this review proposes a reproducible and scalable roadmap for transcriptome analysis in non-model organisms. We also discuss future directions, including the development of inclusive reference databases, AI-driven annotation frameworks, and open, containerized infrastructures aligned with FAIR principles to support global transcriptomics research.

title: Cross-species epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity: Insights from Jonathan the Giant Tortoise and human centenarians
authors: Pischedda, S.; Gomez Carballa, A.; Martinon-Torres, F.; et al.
abstract: Can epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity transcend species boundaries? By comparing findings from a previously published epigenomic study of Jonathan, a 194-year-old giant tortoise, based on buccal scrape and saliva samples, with the analyses of publicly available DNA methylation data from exceptionally long-lived humans based on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), this comparative study reveals intriguing molecular parallels across evolutionarily distant species. Human individuals aged 110+ years exhibited significantly higher global methylation entropy than those aged 60-82 years. Furthermore, 12 candidate genes displayed a distinctive promoter methylation entropy profile, with lower values at the youngest and oldest ages than in intermediate-age groups. Strikingly, these genes were enriched in telomere-related biological processes, highlighting a compelling link between epigenomic patterns and pathways implicated in aging. The correspondence between the findings in humans and previously reported observations in Jonathan suggests testable hypotheses about epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity that may be conserved across species and extend beyond tissue-specific effects.

title: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Reveals Distinct Cellular and Molecular Features of Steroid-Induced Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head Compared to Alcohol-Induced Osteonecrosis and Hip Osteoarthritis
authors: Sarkar, A.; Gallo, M. C.; Bell, J. A.; et al.
abstract: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) remains a devastating complication of glucocorticoid therapy and alcohol abuse, yet the pathophysiology is poorly understood. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed femoral head specimens from patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty due to steroid-induced ONFH, alcohol-induced ONFH, or hip osteoarthritis (OA). Our comprehensive analysis across conditions revealed etiology-specific cellular compositions and transcriptional profiles. Steroid-induced ONFH demonstrated a distinctive immunological signature characterized by a neutrophil-predominant, elevated innate-to-adaptive immune cell ratio compared to alcohol-induced ONFH or OA. T cell analysis revealed impaired maturation in steroid-induced ONFH, with abundant naive T cells but reduced mature CD4+ T cells and CD4+ memory T cells compared to both alcohol-induced ONFH and OA. In addition, compared to alcohol-induced ONFH, steroid-induced ONFH was associated with an increase in exhausted/dysfunctional CD8+ T cells which suggests an impaired response to stress and reflects chronic immune dysfunction. Within stromal cell populations, steroid-induced ONFH demonstrated an increase in pericytes, endothelial cells, and mesenchymal cell with osteogenic features as compared to both alcohol-induced ONFH or OA. These findings collectively reveal novel cellular mechanisms underlying steroid-induced ONFH which may contribute to further investigation of etiology-specific pathogenesis and treatment strategies.

title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
authors: Wang, X.; Zhang, Y.; Chen, S.; et al.
abstract: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.

title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
authors: Cupaioli, F. A.; Merelli, I.
abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

title: Short-read whole-genome sequencing identifies the Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg transgene insertion site on mouse chromosome 4
authors: Wu, X.; Bagish, M. C.; Sanchez Vela, P.; et al.
abstract: Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg, also known as HSC-Scl-CreERT, is a well-used transgenic allele that enables genetic manipulation in mouse hematopoietic cells. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing, we identified the transgene insertion site on chromosome 4 approximately 6 kb upstream of Echdc2.

title: European LD proxies lose tagging for 43% of GWAS leads in the African panel: a chromosome 22 analysis with SwiftLD, an 826-fold faster, byte-identical vcftools LD
authors: Christensen, J.
abstract: SwiftLD is a drop-in replacement for the pairwise linkage disequilibrium (LD) modes of vcftools 0.1.17, --hap-r2 and --geno-r2, which population-genetic pipelines use to compute r2, D and D' between nearby variants. On three regions of 1000 Genomes chromosome 22 with 503 to 2,504 samples it wrote the same output as vcftools, byte for byte, and was 826-fold faster (geometric mean at two threads on an AVX-512 CPU). It was also 7.6-fold faster than PLINK 2, the fastest alternative, from VCF input to LD output on all five regions tested; PLINK 2 writes a different file, although its r2 values agree with vcftools' within 10^-6. One megabase with 503 samples took vcftools 29 s and SwiftLD 0.049 s, and on an ordinary AVX2 laptop SwiftLD was 102-fold faster than vcftools at 12 threads. vcftools was slow because it repeatedly re-reads genotypes from a temporary file, counts haplotypes individually and flushes every output row. I built SwiftLD with correctness-gated coding agents (Claude Opus 5.5): every change had to keep the output byte-identical to vcftools. No output byte differed in 167,749 differential tests on three machines. On chromosome 22, the best European LD proxy of a GWAS lead kept r2 >= 0.8 for 57.4% of leads in the African panel and 85.6% to 92.7% in other panels (98.1% in a European split-half control). Code and a two-command reproduction: https://github.com/joe-b-christensen/swiftld.

title: Synthetic epigenomes for open cross-platform episignature classifiers
authors: Ferraro, F.; Bardina, L.; Drost, M.; et al.
abstract: DNA methylation (DNAm) signature (episignature) classifiers support diagnosis of rare diseases. Yet episignature testing is confined to a dedicated array platform, and most classifiers are neither openly available nor fully reproducible. Laboratories cannot train their own classifiers as positive controls are scarce and cannot be shared under privacy regulations. Here, we develop and release MethaDory, a framework to train episignature classifiers using synthetic DNAm profiles generated in silico from control data and summary statistics of affected individuals from any platform of interest. We trained 188 classifiers spanning 102 rare disorders and validated 154 across 915 individuals with an episignature-associated diagnosis, 533 healthy controls profiled with DNAm arrays, Oxford Nanopore, and PacBio sequencing, together with 7 international centres. MethaDory achieved an average F1 0.9 on arrays, matching or outperforming existing approaches. We show MethaDory classifier application to long-read genome data, facilitating diagnoses in unsolved cases and in ultra-rapid diagnostic settings.

title: Genomic and Epigenomic Relationships Capture Different Patterns of Genotype-by-Environment Interaction in Grapevine Clones
authors: Robinson, H.; Schmidt, M.; Callipo, P.; et al.
abstract: Genotype-by-environment interaction (GEI) challenges selection in clonally propagated perennial crops by reducing the consistency of clone performance across years. In perennial crops, both genetic and epigenetic variation are likely to contribute to complex trait variation among clones. However, the extent to which each molecular source contribute to GEI remains poorly understood. Here, we used UMR-seq, an assay that recovers SNPs and unmethylated-region (UMR; DNA methylation) profiles from a single library, to generate paired genomic and epigenomic profiles for 206 Riesling (Vitis vinifera L.) clones phenotyped for yield and juice quality traits across nine growing seasons. We then partitioned the contribution of each omic layer to clonal variation and GEI, and examined the genomic distribution of their effects. In models without explicit GEI, environmental and residual effects were the largest source of phenotypic variance and the clonal main effect was modest. Genomic relationships accounted for most of the clonal variance in four of five traits, and adding an epigenomic relationship matrix (ERM) to the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) had little effect. In contrast, when GEI effects were modelled using factor-analytic covariance structures, the epigenomic layer captured a substantial proportion of GEI variance and exceeded the genomic contribution in four of five traits. The two omic layers differed not only in the amount of GEI captured, but also in the pattern of clone re-ranking across years. When back-solved effects were aggregated into genomic windows, the largest genomic and epigenomic effects tended to fall in different regions, with overlap no greater than expected by chance. Together, these results show that genomic and epigenomic relationships capture complementary components of year-to-year variation in clone performance, with the epigenomic contribution expressed primarily through GEI. These findings provide a basis for investigating the molecular drivers of GEI and for testing whether genomic and epigenomic information can inform selection for stable clonal performance across variable environments.

title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
authors: Islam, U. I.; Marsico, F.; Garrison, E.; et al.
abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries. GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once. On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.
